SPQ1.notes: Only one trial in this group. The participant used the right approach (find 161 on the x-axis, go up to the point, read its weight) but anchored on the 166 cm column, which is next to the sparse lower-left points, and read about 58 kg. They noticed the slip themselves afterwards. What matters on this item is the lone bottom-left point at (161, 44) and placing 161 between the 160 and 165 ticks.

SPQ3.question: What is the range in weight for the 85 individuals?
SPQ3.reference_chain: MAP(weight → yaxis) → ARGMIN({pt[*]}, y)=pt[161cm,44.4kg] → ARGMAX({pt[*]}, y)=pt[176.8cm,74kg] → PROJ(both → yaxis) → READ(y)≈44.4, ≈74 → RANGE(44,74)
SPQ3.notes: The main split is between data extent and axis extent. Six of the 13 trials used extent-of-data (horizontal projections from the lowest and highest points to the weight axis, giving 44 to 74). Four circled or traced the axis end ticks (40 and 75). One switched to the height variable (161 to 182). The recorded accuracy is 0 for every scored trial, even those answering 44/74, which matches the stated correct range. This looks like a scoring artifact, so n_correct is low for that reason and not because of reasoning errors. The isolated extreme points (161,44) and (177,74) are the pivotal elements.

SPQ4.question: There is a group of individuals centered at the height of 176 cm and the weight of 55 kg. True or False?
SPQ4.reference_chain: FIND(xtick[176]) → FIND(ytick[55]) → PROJ(both → chart) → LOOK(region[176cm,55kg]) → COUNT({pt} in region)=0 → GROUP({pt[*]}) shows dense cluster near (170-174, 55-60) → CMP(cluster center ? (176,55)) → ANSWER(False)
SPQ4.notes: Most participants (34/39) answered False. The dominant gesture was a crosshair: a horizontal line from 55 kg and a vertical line from 176 cm meeting at an empty spot, sometimes circled. Variants were circling the empty region directly, projecting only vertically, or drawing outward arrows from a circled spot to both axes as a check. Errors came from reading 'centered at' loosely (accepting points along the 176 column or nearby as a group), from not knowing how many points make a group, and from stopping short when locating 176, which is not a labelled tick. Few participants located the real dense cluster (170-175 cm, 55-60 kg).

SPQ5.question: There is a negative linear relationship between the height and the weight of the 85 individuals. True or False?
SPQ5.reference_chain: SCAN({pt[*]}) → FIT(trendline) → SLOPE(trendline) > 0 → CORR(height,weight)=+ → CMP(+ ? −) → ANSWER(False)
SPQ5.notes: Drawing a freehand upward trendline through the cloud was by far the most common strategy (19 trendlines), and nearly all of those answered False. Three drew the correct upward line but still answered True or 'not sure', so seeing the trend and mapping its sign to the claim are separate steps. Most failures were vocabulary confusion about 'negative linear' with no reading of the chart, or reasoning from a couple of extreme points (the tallest-but-light outlier, the lightest person) instead of the overall trend. Rare strategies: an upper/lower envelope, a staircase of sampled point projections, and a drawn negative-slope template compared against the cloud.

new_symbols.FIT(trendline): draw or imagine a best-fit line through a point set (sketch: a freehand line through the cloud)
new_symbols.DRAW(template[...]): draw a reference shape (e.g. what a negative slope would look like) to compare against the data
new_symbols.trendline[↗]: the participant-drawn trend line, with direction arrow
new_symbols.envelope[upper|lower]: a boundary line drawn along the upper or lower edge of a point cloud
new_symbols.template[↘]: a drawn hypothetical pattern, not fitted to the data

SPQ6.question: What is the height of the most prominent outlier in the data?
SPQ6.reference_chain: SCAN({pt[*]}) → FIT(trendline ↗) → OUTLIER({pt[*]} | distance from trend) = pt[181.6cm,45.8kg] → PROJ(pt → xaxis) → INTERP(x | ticks 180,185) → READ(x)≈181.6 → ANSWER(≈182)
SPQ6.notes: Accuracy was not recorded for any trial. Only two participants (2/9) picked the true outlier, the tall-but-light point at (181.6 cm, 45.8 kg), and both then entered its weight (46) and corrected themselves in the text. Most people took 'most prominent outlier' to mean an extreme on one axis: the topmost point (176-177 cm, 74 kg) or the shortest and lightest point (161 cm, 44 kg). One chose the densest column. The pivotal element is spotting distance from the positive trend, which no one described explicitly.
